newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean unions reject offer of TV debate, clashes.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean unions reject offer of TV debate, clashes.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party chief challenged union leaders on Saturday to a televised debate over a controversial new labour law, in a dramatic change of tack to try to turn public opinion against strikers.
But leaders of the country's two major umbrella union groups brushed aside the offer as a propaganda ploy.

Within hours of the proposal, about 20,000 workers calling for the resignation of President Kim Young-sam clashed with riot police in central Seoul, in the most violent street protest since the labour bill was rammed through parliament on December 26.
Witnesses said the protesters used iron bars to rip up paving stones and fought a running battle with riot police who fired tear gas to stop them marching on Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.

They wanted to join seven leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, who are camped out in a makeshift plastic tent pitched on the grounds of the cathedral beneath a statue of the Virgin Mary.

Earlier, international labour officials visited the union leaders in a gesture of worker solidarity. Their visit highlighted mounting overseas criticism of the law, which has sparked two weeks of nationwide strikes.

New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo invited union leaders to go on air for a live debate over the law, which allows companies to lay off workers and hire temporary staff to break strikes, shattering a jobs-for-life labour tradition. Lee said workers' anger largely stemmed from misunderstandings.

Public opinion is seen as a make-or-break factor in the stoppages, which have closed car plants and disrupted hospitals. Unions have threatened the biggest strike in the nation's history next Tuesday and Wednesday.
Lee's offer contrasted with angry face-offs before dawn on Saturday, when police trying to arrest seven confederation leaders were turned away by workers armed with iron bars.
Amid other signs that the government was trying to avoid confrontation and seek dialogue, Lee told reporters he would meet any union leader.
He made clear, though, the government had no intention of revising the law.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil rejected Lee's offer, saying the government should first scrap the law.
"Unless the government makes concessions, all-out strikes are inevitable," said Kwon, whose confederation claims half a million members.

A leader of the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the largest umbrella union group with 1.2 million members, said: "Unless the new law is repealed, we will not be part of the government's propaganda."

Unions denounce the legislation as an "evil law", and international labour organisations have said it is even harsher than the law it replaced. Seoul officials say the law is needed to rescue the economy from a worrying downturn.

"I've spoken to labour officials and there have been a lot of misunderstandings. That's why we proposed discussing the issue openly through a television debate," a party spokesman quoted Lee as telling local reporters.
"Chairman Lee said the party does not want to resolve everything by mobilising official forces," the spokesman said.
A prosecution source said state prosecutors were negotiating with church officials to find a way to serve the arrest warrants on the seven union leaders peacefully.
On Saturday the union leader too appeared to back away from violent confrontation, shaken by an attempted suicide by a Hyundai car worker on Friday who set himself on fire.

Marcello Malantacchi, secretary general of the International Metalworkers' Federation, and Guy Rider, who heads the Geneva office of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), attacked the law as an assault on fundamental rights.
